must_remember: Curl of a vector field is defined as the vector cross product of the del operator with the vector field: $\nabla \times V$.
A mechanical force field $F$ is conservative if and only if its curl is identically zero everywhere: $\nabla \times F = 0$.
For a rigid body rotating with a uniform angular velocity $\omega$, the curl of the linear velocity field equals twice the angular velocity: $\nabla \times v = 2\omega$.
The curl of the gradient of any scalar field is identically zero: $\nabla \times (\nabla \phi) = 0$.
The divergence of the curl of any vector field is identically zero: $\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times V) = 0$.
Stokes' theorem relates the surface integral of the curl of a vector field to the line integral around the bounding contour: $\oint_C F \cdot dr = \iint_S (\nabla \times F) \cdot dS$.

glossary.meaning: A vector operator that describes the infinitesimal rotation of a vector field in 3D space, denoted by $\nabla \times V$.
A vector field whose curl is zero everywhere ($\nabla \times V = 0$), implying it has no local circulation or vorticity.
A force with the property that the total work done in moving between two points is independent of the taken path, equivalent to having a zero curl ($\nabla \times F = 0$).
A pseudovector ($\omega$) pointing along the axis of rotation whose magnitude is the rate of angular rotation.
An inertial force proportional to $-2 \omega \times v$ experienced in a rotating reference frame.
